901.quote_or_event: “For a fool who is bound in the fetters of sensuality will be subject to delusion again and again.”
901.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on women says that a man bound by sensual attachment keeps falling back into delusion (moha), which in Jain terms binds fresh karma and blocks liberation.
901.tie_back: Like Kural 901, it says that a man given over to desire for a woman loses life's highest goal, which for Jainism is moksha.
901._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The verse is addressed to monks tempted by women, not to husbands, so it shares the Kural's theme of attachment costing the higher goal but not its household setting.

902.quote_or_event: “Getting up in the night they lull the baby asleep like nurses; and though they are ashamed of themselves, they wash the clothes like washermen.”
902.explanation: The text pictures a man who fell for a woman and now does every household chore, aware of his own shame but unable to stop.
902.tie_back: This matches Kural 902, where a man who neglects his own standing out of desire for his wife ends up publicly ashamed.
902._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (footnote markers omitted). The context is a monk who abandoned his vows, and its picture of 'shameful' domestic work reflects ancient ascetic and gender assumptions.

903.quote_or_event: “When a monk breaks the law, dotes (on a woman), and is absorbed by that passion, she afterwards scolds him, lifts her foot, and tramples on his head.”
903.explanation: The Sutrakritanga shows what doting leads to: the infatuated man ends up humbled and dominated by the woman he gave way to.
903.tie_back: It closely matches Kural 903's 'unnatural' stooping in fear before one's wife, which shames a man among good people.
903._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (footnote marker omitted). The image of the doting, dominated man is very close to the Kural, though here the man is a lapsed monk, not a householder.

904.quote_or_event: “His father and mother, his children and wife who claim him, will admonish him: 'See, you are our supporter; care not for the next world in order to support us.'”
904.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that family, wife included, can pull a person away from the merit and discipline that shape his next existence.
904.tie_back: Kural 904 says the man ruled by fear of his wife becomes marumai-ilaalan, 'one without the next world', and this verse shows that same pull from the Jain side.
904._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Close on losing the next world, but the claim comes from the whole family, not only the wife, and the scene is someone tempted back from renunciation.

905.quote_or_event: Among Hemachandra's thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder is 'Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt', rendered by Sangave as diligent in helping ascetics, the righteous and the needy. It goes with the lay vow of atithi-samvibhaga, sharing one's food with ascetics.
905.explanation: In Jainism, a householder is expected to look after ascetics, good people and guests freely and as a regular duty.
905.tie_back: Kural 905 condemns the wife-fearing man who hesitates to do good to good people (the commentator lists ascetics and guests), which is exactly the duty Hemachandra's householder must not neglect.
905.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, list of 35 householder qualities, no. 19, as rendered in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com)
905._accuracy_note: Wording checked on Sangave's jainworld page, paraphrased here. It states the positive duty, so it is only a partial match: it does not mention a wife or fear.

906.quote_or_event: “This has been done by many men who for the sake of pleasures have stooped so low; they become the equals of slaves, animals, servants, beasts of burden--mere nobodies.”
906.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says men who give themselves over to a woman for pleasure lose every bit of standing and become 'mere nobodies'.
906.tie_back: This is Kural 906's point that men who fear their wife's arms have no paatu, no real dignity, however splendidly they live.
906._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The loss of dignity matches well, but the Kural's contrast with god-like splendour has no parallel here.

907.quote_or_event: “But when they have captured him, they send him on all sorts of errands.”
907.explanation: A long passage of the Sutrakritanga then lists the woman's orders (fetch fruit, rub my back, bring the mirror) and says such women 'order their husbands about like slaves' (1.4.2.15).
907.tie_back: It is nearly a one-to-one match for Kural 907's man who 'conducts himself doing a woman's errands' (pen-eval).
907._accuracy_note: Both phrases verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The errand-running image is the same as the Kural's, though Jacobi's text speaks of a lapsed monk and has a satirical, misogynistic tone.

908.quote_or_event: “Some people are (foolishly) attached to others, and are thereby deluded; the unrighteous make them adopt unrighteousness, and they exult in their wickedness.”
908.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that foolish attachment to another person can draw a man away from right conduct altogether.
908.tie_back: Kural 908 says men who live only as their wives wish neither help their friends nor do good deeds, and this verse gives the general Jain diagnosis behind that failure.
908._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, but it is generic: it does not name a wife and does not mention friends. Next-best match only.

909.quote_or_event: Hemachandra lists as a quality of the ideal Jain householder 'Anyonya-pratibandhena trivargam sadhayan', which Sangave renders as fulfilling the three-fold aim of life (dharma, artha and kama) without excluding any of its elements.
909.explanation: Jain lay ethics asks a householder to pursue virtue, wealth and pleasure in balance so that none crowds out the others.
909.tie_back: Kural 909 says the man who obeys his wife in everything loses all three, aram, porul and inbam, which is the same trivarga the Jain householder is told to keep in balance.
909.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, list of 35 householder qualities, no. 18, as rendered in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com)
909._accuracy_note: Wording verified on Sangave's jainworld page and paraphrased. The three aims match the Kural exactly, but the Jain text gives the positive ideal rather than warning against wife-domination.

910.quote_or_event: “Restraining himself by the thought that these dangerous (pleasures) will not be to his benefit, a monk should abstain from women.”
910.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's remedy is reflection: a man who thinks clearly about what harms him keeps himself from falling under a woman's sway.
910.tie_back: Kural 910 likewise says that people whose minds are joined to deliberation (en-serndha nenjam) never fall into the folly of being ruled by a woman.
910._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the verse continues with a further prohibition, omitted here). The protective role of reflection matches, but the Kural's mention of statecraft and wealth (idan) has no Jain parallel.
